quiz_support_facts: Path("notes/sky.txt") constructs a path description. Constructing it does not create a folder or a file.

```python
from pathlib import Path
p = Path("drafts/sea.log")
print(p.name)
print(p.with_suffix(".md"))
```
The path ending in sea.md is a new path description; the original p still ends in sea.log.
with_suffix replaces only the last suffix. For archive.tar.gz, replacing it with .md gives archive.tar.md. A name with no suffix gains .md.
Path methods such as read_text and write_text perform real file operations, unlike this exercise. Do not call them here.
datetime contains tools for calendar dates and times. This lesson uses date for a calendar day, not a moment with a timezone.
timedelta(days=1) represents a one-day difference. Adding it to a date follows calendar boundaries instead of adding to the characters in a string.

```python
from datetime import date, timedelta
day = date.fromisoformat("2026-04-30")
later = day + timedelta(days=1)
print(later.isoformat())
```
The result is 2026-05-01. isoformat converts the date back to year-month-day text.
from collections import Counter imports a dictionary-like counting tool. Counter counts each distinct value from an input collection.

```python
from collections import Counter
counts = Counter(["art", "music", "art"])
print(counts["art"])
print(counts["dance"])
```
The outputs are 2 and 0. Reading a missing Counter key returns zero rather than raising a missing-key error.
dict(counts) converts the stored counts to an ordinary dictionary. After conversion, ordinary dictionary rules apply; a missing key is no longer automatically zero.
defaultdict(list) uses list as a factory: it calls list() to create a fresh empty list for each new key. Pass list, not list().

```python
from collections import defaultdict
groups = defaultdict(list)
groups["art"].append("Sketch")
groups["music"].append("Sing")
print(dict(groups))
```
The two categories own different lists. Adding to art does not add to music.
For category, title in rows unpacks each pair into two names. Append each title to groups[category] as you visit it; append preserves order and duplicates.
json.dumps converts a supported Python value into JSON text. json.loads goes the other direction, from JSON text to Python data.

```python
import json
text = json.dumps({"ready": True, "title": "Café"}, ensure_ascii=False, sort_keys=True)
print(text)
```
JSON represents Python True as true. This returns a string, not a saved file.
Use json.dumps instead of assembling JSON with string concatenation. A title containing quotes or a newline needs correct escaping.

Parsing the exported text with json.loads should recover the same supported data. Do not serialize a Python object by just calling str(note): Python’s printed dictionary is not the same format as JSON.

```python
import random
rng = random.Random(7)
print(rng.choice(["draw", "read", "walk"]))
```
Random creates a separate generator. A seed chooses its starting state; the same seed and same sequence of calls can repeat results in the same environment.
choice selects one element from a nonempty sequence. It can choose the same value on consecutive calls; randomness does not promise alternation.
Passing rng into your function lets a caller control or test the choices. Do not reset it on every call: that would keep restarting its sequence.
[A-Z] matches one ASCII uppercase letter. [0-9] matches one ASCII digit. A count in braces, such as {2}, requires exactly two repetitions of the preceding pattern.
fullmatch succeeds only when the entire string fits. It returns a match object on success and None on failure. Comparing the result with None produces a Boolean.
A substring match is not enough. ABC-42-extra contains a valid-looking beginning but must fail the whole-string rule. This small pattern is not a general validator for arbitrary identifiers.
An iterable can supply values one at a time. An iterator remembers where it has reached; iter(items) creates an iterator from an iterable, and next(iterator) obtains its next value.

```python
from itertools import islice
stream = iter(["A", "B", "C"])
preview = list(islice(stream, 2))
print(preview)
print(next(stream))
```
The preview is ["A", "B"]. The next stream value is "C" because the first two have already been consumed.
list collects the selected finite portion into a list. Put islice inside list, not list around the unlimited original stream.
An iterator is not automatically restarted after a preview. Reusing it continues from its current position. A fresh iterator is a different object.
